terms.gloss: science; the systematic knowledge of a field
evidence: Cic. Fin. 1.63: In physicīs plūrimum posuit. eā scientiā …
M-O s.v. science (natural sciences): scientia nātūrālis, after Pallas (1811)
terms.comment: Classically the knowing of a thing, usually with the genitive of the field: scientia jūris, reī mīlitāris (Cicero, Lewis & Short). The sciences are scientiae, a plural Lewis & Short finds only in Vitruvius; the natural sciences, scientia nātūrālis or disciplīnae nātūrālēs (Morgan–Owens, after Pallas and Egger).

terms.gloss: natural science, the study of nature
evidence: Cic. Fin. 1.17: in physicīs … tōtus est aliēnus
terms.comment: Cicero’s word for the science of nature, from the Greek; also physica or physicē, feminine (Fin. 3.72–73). In modern Latin it is physics. A scientist is physicus: physicum, id est speculātōrem vēnātōremque nātūrae (Cic. ND 1.83).

phrases.latin: In physicīs plūrimum posuit. … omnium autem rērum nātūrā cognitā levāmur superstitiōne, līberāmur mortis metū
phrases.english: He set the greatest store by natural science. … Once we know the nature of all things, we are freed from superstition and from the fear of death

phrases.latin: physicum, id est speculātōrem vēnātōremque nātūrae
phrases.english: a scientist, that is, an observer and hunter of nature

sources: Lewis & Short: scientia · Lewis & Short: physica · Lewis & Short: physicus
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. science (natural sciences); scientist.
Cicero’s De finibus and De natura deorum, and Vitruvius, checked against the Perseus Latin texts (9 November 2026).
Traupman has no word for science.
